argument: Adam Smith argues that true wealth isn't a raw dollar figure but what your labor can actually buy, and that this real wealth has exploded because of specialization and self-interested trade. People pursuing their own interests, not altruism, is what has made ordinary modern life more comfortable than that of history's kings.
keyIdeas: Wealth should be measured by what your money or labor can actually buy, not just a raw number -- illustrated by the 'million dollars vs. a cheeseburger' desert-island example.

Real wealth, measured in labor-hours needed for an hour of light, increased over 43,000-fold in 200 years because technological innovation and specialization reinforce each other in a self-perpetuating cycle.
Smith's pin-factory example shows specialization lets a team of workers produce tens of thousands of times more than a single generalist working alone could ever manage.
Trying to do everything yourself, like carrying a Swiss Army knife instead of separate specialized tools, produces mediocre versions of everything rather than a few genuinely good things.

Smith reframes self-interest: people don't need to be altruistic for society to benefit -- appealing to someone's self-interest, as in trade or Steve Jobs building the iPhone, can produce broad social good regardless of the underlying motive.

terms.def: Dividing labor so individuals or groups focus on one task, dramatically increasing output and quality.

Smith's actual term for what the episode calls 'specialization': the pin-factory example of breaking production into over a dozen separate steps done by different workers, letting a team make ~50,000 pins a day versus one person's single pin.
Acting in one's own benefit; Smith argues this, not altruism, is what drives people to make bargains that end up benefiting society.

terms.term: "Man is an animal that makes bargains"
terms.def: Smith's phrase for the human habit of trading by appealing to others' self-interest rather than their charity.
Wealth measured by what your labor or money can actually purchase, rather than a raw net-worth figure.
